newsitem.title: UK: UK petrol war shuts nearly 10 pct of sites.
newsitem.headline: UK petrol war shuts nearly 10 pct of sites.

text.p: A severe price war in the U.K. petrol market, aggravated by Esso's Pricewatch campaign, led to a near 10 percent reduction in the number of sites in 1996 and underscored a competitive environment for this year, industry analysts said on Friday.
The Institute of Petroleum (IP), a trade group, said 1,496 petrol stations closed last year, nearly double the rate of the previous year to leave a total of 14,478 sites.
"The period of restructuring precipitated by the price war hasn't ended yet," said Stephen Brooks, principal consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh.

"The consumer is still benefiting from very competitive prices and nothing has changed our view about margins -- they will remain tight," he said. "I wouldn't say it's good news or bad news. It depends on whose perspective you're looking at it from."

Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, remained the market leader with 1,980 sites, but the major oil companies still shed sites last year at the expense of the supermarket outlets, which grew by 6.5 percent, the IP said.
Esso's pledge early last year to match its lowest-priced competitor was a bonus for motorists, keeping U.K. pump prices amongst the lowest in Europe.
But margins were squeezed to break-even levels at the height of the price war last summer, forcing the higher-cost independent retailers out of business.
The emergence of the supermarkets who have lower costs for selling petrol and a chronic overcapacity in the U.K. have also led to the closures, analysts said.
Some analysts warned that reduced competition in rural areas would be bad news for those consumers.
Royal Dutch/Shell held the second slot with 1,706 sites, down 199 from 1995, the IP said.
The survey, conducted at the end of 1996, provides "proof of the difficulties caused by last year's petrol price war and the continuing struggle to make profits," it said.

Gross fuel margins sank to as low as two pence per litre last summer but have since recovered, and many analysts and oil companies said they expect them to hold between four and five pence per litre. That is still below pre-Pricewatch levels of six to eight pence.

"I don't necessarily think that we'll see quite as many closures (in 1997) because prices have picked up a bit and margins today are better than at the height of the price war," another energy consultant said.
"If a Tesco or a Sainsbury opens a petrol outlet in an area...that might cause two other outlets to fail because the volume that goes through a supermarket is very high," he said.
Analysts have said that while Pricewatch may have been intended to narrow price differentials between filling stations, it may actually increase the price variances between rural and urban areas.
"It's a lot of little local wars instead of a giant battle," the consultant said.
